# Cost Optimization and Scaling Strategies

##### ₹11.4 lakh a month for a summarise button

A SaaS company in Pune added an AI summarisation feature. Six weeks later the finance team escalated: the OpenAI bill was ₹11.4 lakh a month, against a product line generating ₹9 lakh.

The breakdown, once someone instrumented it:

| Cause | Share of spend |
|---|---|
| Every request to GPT-4-class model, including trivial ones | 48% |
| No caching — the same 40 documents summarised repeatedly | 21% |
| A 2,200-token system prompt on every call | 18% |
| Retries on timeout, re-billing the full prompt | 8% |
| Genuinely necessary complex summarisation | 5% |

Only 5% of spend was doing irreplaceable work. Routing simple requests to a small model, adding exact and semantic caching, trimming the system prompt, and fixing the retry logic brought the bill to ₹1.3 lakh — an 89% reduction with no measurable quality change on their evaluation set.

Cost optimisation in AI is not belt-tightening. It is usually the discovery that most of your spend is doing nothing.

##### Know your cost drivers

For self-hosted GPU inference:

```
cost per 1M tokens = (GPU ₹/hour ÷ 3600) × (1M ÷ tokens_per_second) ÷ utilization
```

Three multipliers hide in that formula, and utilisation is the one people miss. An A100 at ₹210/hour running at 25% utilisation costs 4× per token what the same GPU costs at 100%. Before optimising the model, check whether the GPU is even busy — the answer is frequently no.

For API-based LLMs, the levers are: which model, input tokens, output tokens (usually priced 2–4× higher than input), number of calls, and retries. Note that output tokens dominate on generation-heavy workloads and input tokens dominate on RAG — the optimisation differs accordingly.

You cannot optimise what you do not measure, so instrument first:

```python
from prometheus_client import Counter, Histogram

COST = Counter("llm_cost_inr_total", "", ["model", "tenant", "feature", "cache"])
TOKENS = Counter("llm_tokens_total", "", ["model", "direction"])

PRICING_INR = {   # per 1K tokens, indicative
    "gpt-4o":       {"in": 0.42, "out": 1.68},
    "gpt-4o-mini":  {"in": 0.025, "out": 0.10},
    "claude-haiku": {"in": 0.033, "out": 0.166},
    "self-hosted-7b": {"in": 0.004, "out": 0.004},
}

def record(model, feature, tenant, in_tok, out_tok, cache_hit=False):
    p = PRICING_INR[model]
    cost = 0.0 if cache_hit else (in_tok / 1000 * p["in"] + out_tok / 1000 * p["out"])
    COST.labels(model, tenant, feature, str(cache_hit)).inc(cost)
    TOKENS.labels(model, "in").inc(in_tok); TOKENS.labels(model, "out").inc(out_tok)
    return cost
```

Track cost **per feature and per tenant**, not just in aggregate. Aggregate spend tells you there is a problem; per-feature spend tells you where.

##### Model routing: the largest single lever

Chen et al.'s FrugalGPT showed that cascading from cheap to expensive models can cut cost 90%+ while matching or beating the strong model's accuracy. The reason is simple: most requests are easy.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
import re

@dataclass
class Route:
    model: str
    max_tokens: int

class Router:
    """Cascade: try cheap, escalate on low confidence or explicit difficulty."""

    def classify(self, req) -> str:
        text = req.prompt
        # Cheap heuristics first — a classifier call costs money too
        if len(text) < 400 and not re.search(r"\b(analyse|compare|why|explain|derive)\b", text, re.I):
            return "simple"
        if req.requires_tools or req.needs_multi_step:
            return "complex"
        if len(text) > 8000:
            return "long_context"
        return "medium"

    def route(self, req) -> Route:
        return {
            "simple":       Route("self-hosted-7b", 512),
            "medium":       Route("gpt-4o-mini", 1024),
            "complex":      Route("gpt-4o", 2048),
            "long_context": Route("claude-haiku", 4096),
        }[self.classify(req)]

async def generate_with_cascade(req, router, judge_threshold=0.7):
    route = router.route(req)
    out = await call(route.model, req, max_tokens=route.max_tokens)
    if route.model != "gpt-4o":
        score = await cheap_quality_check(req, out)      # small model or heuristic
        if score < judge_threshold:
            ESCALATIONS.inc()
            out = await call("gpt-4o", req, max_tokens=2048)
    return out
```

Two disciplines make routing safe. **Measure the escalation rate** — if it exceeds about 20%, your cheap tier is too weak and you are paying for both calls. And **evaluate the routed system as a whole** against an eval set, not just the individual models; a router that sends 8% of hard queries to a weak model has a quality problem that per-model metrics hide.

LiteLLM is worth adopting here — one interface across providers, with built-in fallbacks, retries, budgets and cost tracking:

```python
from litellm import Router
router = Router(
    model_list=[
        {"model_name": "cheap", "litellm_params": {"model": "gpt-4o-mini"},
         "tpm": 2_000_000},
        {"model_name": "strong", "litellm_params": {"model": "gpt-4o"}, "tpm": 300_000},
    ],
    fallbacks=[{"cheap": ["strong"]}],
    routing_strategy="usage-based-routing-v2",
    enable_pre_call_checks=True,
)
```

##### Caching: three tiers

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q[Request] --> E{Exact hash in Redis?}
    E -->|Hit ~15-30%| R1[Return, cost 0]
    E -->|Miss| S{Semantic similarity > 0.95?}
    S -->|Hit ~10-20%| R2[Return cached, cost = 1 embedding]
    S -->|Miss| P{Shared prefix cached?}
    P -->|Yes| R3[Prefill reused: 50-90% off input tokens]
    P -->|No| F[Full inference]
    F --> W[Write both caches]
```

**Exact caching** hashes the full request (model, prompt, all sampling parameters) and is free money on deterministic requests. Real-world hit rates of 15–30% are typical, because user traffic is heavily repetitive.

**Semantic caching** embeds the query and returns a cached answer above a similarity threshold. Powerful for FAQ-shaped traffic, and genuinely risky — at 0.90 similarity, "what is the refund policy for electronics" can match "what is the refund policy for apparel". Set the threshold at 0.95+, scope the cache per tenant and per document-version, and validate on real query pairs before trusting it.

**Prompt/prefix caching** is provider-side (Anthropic, OpenAI, and vLLM's `enable_prefix_caching`) and reuses the prefill for a shared prefix. With a 2,000-token system prompt on every request, this cuts input cost by 50–90% and slashes TTFT. It requires putting the static content **first** in your prompt, which is a free architectural choice most teams get wrong by interleaving.

```python
import hashlib, json

def exact_key(req: dict) -> str:
    keyed = {k: req[k] for k in ("model", "prompt", "temperature", "top_p", "max_tokens")}
    keyed["prompt_version"] = PROMPT_VERSION      # invalidate on prompt change!
    return "llm:" + hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(keyed, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
```

Including the prompt version in the key is the detail that prevents serving stale answers after a deploy — a subtle bug that looks like the model regressing.

##### Batching and quantization

Both were covered in depth on earlier days; here is what they mean for the bill.

**Continuous batching** (vLLM) raises throughput 5–20× on mixed workloads, which is a proportional reduction in cost per token. Nothing else in this article gives a larger single improvement for self-hosted models.

**Quantization** to 4-bit shrinks weights ~4×. Because decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, that is typically a 2–3× throughput gain *and* it frees VRAM for a larger KV cache, which allows a bigger batch — compounding into a 3–5× effective cost reduction with negligible quality loss when calibrated on your own data.

**Offline batch APIs** deserve a mention: OpenAI and Anthropic both offer roughly 50% discounts for asynchronous batch jobs with a 24-hour SLA. Any workload that is not user-facing — nightly enrichment, backfills, evaluation runs, synthetic data generation — should be on the batch tier. This is often a free 50% on a meaningful slice of spend.

##### Infrastructure levers

| Lever | Saving | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| Spot / preemptible GPUs | 60–90% | Preemption — needs checkpointing |
| Reserved / committed use | 30–55% | Lock-in for 1–3 years |
| Scale-to-zero (KEDA) for dev and batch | ~100% when idle | Cold start 3–10 min |
| Right-sizing (L4 instead of A100) | 40–70% | Requires load testing to confirm |
| Regional selection (asia-south1) | Varies | Latency and data residency |
| Autoscaling on queue depth | 30–50% | Cold-start latency during spikes |

**Right-sizing is the most under-used lever.** A 7B quantised model does not need an A100-80GB; an L4 at roughly a quarter the price often serves it at adequate throughput. The only way to know is a load test that establishes tokens-per-second and p95 latency at your target concurrency on each candidate instance type. Do that test once, and it usually pays for itself many times over.

Spot instances are excellent for training (with frequent checkpointing) and questionable for user-facing inference. A hybrid — a reserved baseline for steady traffic, spot for burst — captures most of the saving with bounded risk.

##### FinOps for ML

Cost has to become a first-class engineering metric, visible in the same place as latency:

- **Attribution.** Tag every resource and every request with team, feature, tenant and environment. Kubecost or OpenCost for infrastructure; your own counters for API spend.
- **Unit economics.** Track ₹ per request, per active user, per resolved ticket. Absolute spend rising with usage is fine; unit cost rising is not.
- **Budgets and hard caps.** Per-tenant token quotas, per-feature daily spend limits, and automated alerts at 50%, 80% and 100%. LLM cost incidents move fast — an infinite agent loop can spend a month's budget overnight.
- **Cost in code review.** A PR that adds 600 tokens to a system prompt should surface the projected monthly delta, the same way it surfaces test coverage.
- **Weekly review.** Top spenders by feature and tenant, week-over-week change, unit cost trend, and cache hit rate.

```python
DAILY_CAPS_INR = {"summarise": 12_000, "chat": 40_000, "agent": 8_000}

async def guard_budget(feature: str, projected_cost: float, redis):
    key = f"budget:{feature}:{date.today()}"
    spent = float(await redis.get(key) or 0)
    cap = DAILY_CAPS_INR[feature]
    if spent + projected_cost > cap:
        if spent > cap * 1.0:
            raise BudgetExceeded(f"{feature} daily cap ₹{cap} reached")
        alert(f"{feature} at {spent/cap:.0%} of daily budget")
    await redis.incrbyfloat(key, projected_cost)
    await redis.expire(key, 172800)
```

##### Common mistakes

- No per-feature cost attribution, so optimisation is guesswork.
- One frontier model for every request, regardless of difficulty.
- No caching at all — typically leaving 20–40% on the table.
- Semantic cache threshold too low, serving confidently wrong answers.
- Cache keys omitting the prompt version, serving stale output after a deploy.
- Dynamic content placed before static content, defeating prefix caching.
- Retries that re-bill the full prompt without a budget cap.
- User-facing hardware for batch workloads that could use the 50% batch API tier.
- Provisioning an A100 without load-testing an L4.
- Measuring absolute spend instead of unit cost, so efficiency gains are invisible under growth.

##### Hands-on

Instrument an existing LLM feature with per-request cost tracking broken down by model, feature and cache status, and produce a one-week breakdown like the table at the top of this article. Then apply three optimisations — exact caching, a two-tier router with an escalation path, and prompt restructuring for prefix caching — and quantify each one's saving independently. Verify quality is unchanged on a held-out eval set; a cost reduction that degrades quality is not a saving.

For the mini-project, build a cost-optimised LLM serving setup: LiteLLM or a custom router with a cheap tier, an escalation path and measured escalation rate; three-tier caching with hit-rate metrics; a quantised self-hosted model on right-sized hardware validated by load test; autoscaling on queue depth with a scale-to-zero dev environment; per-tenant budgets with hard caps; and a dashboard showing cost per request over time, unit cost per active user, cache hit rate and escalation rate. Include a before-and-after cost report. Then write your three-strategy answer on reducing LLM cost without hurting quality, with your own measured numbers behind each.

##### Key takeaways

- Measure cost per feature and per tenant first; most AI bills are dominated by work that did not need doing.
- Model routing with a cheap first tier and a measured escalation rate is typically the single largest saving.
- Caching compounds: exact, semantic (at a strict threshold), and prefix — and prefix caching requires static content first.
- Continuous batching and 4-bit quantization together give 3–5× on self-hosted cost with negligible quality loss.
- Track unit cost, not absolute spend, and put hard per-feature budget caps in the request path.
